prize_parts.citation: For the discovery that biomolecular phase separation organizes the interior of living cells

statement.case_for: Biomolecular condensation brought classical phase behaviour, multivalency and thermodynamics into cell biology and gave a general physical-chemical principle for how cells organize their interior without membranes. The 2009 P-granule work of Hyman and Brangwynne, together with Rosen's multivalent-interaction framework for signalling assemblies, defined a concept that is now used to frame nucleolar assembly, stress granules, transcriptional control and aggregation disease. It is a new concept of molecular organisation rather than a tool, it has about fifteen years of independent confirmation across many systems, and it is the physical-chemistry and soft-matter contribution on a list otherwise dominated by synthesis, chemical biology and methods.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that physiological relevance is still disputed: many in vitro condensates may reflect overexpression, crowding or concentration artefacts, and demonstrating that phase separation, rather than another assembly mechanism, causes a given function is hard. Credit is also not cleanly separable among Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag, and a Chemistry framing has to be argued against a Physiology or Medicine one. Opening support is thin: only I ranked it first, and Heiner Linke placed it sixth. I should not read that as a verdict on its merit, but it does show how far from consensus it is.

responses.point: Linke ranks base editing (B060) first as a conceptually clean chemical principle, an engineered deaminase on a programmable nickase, that is easy to explain and has a large therapeutic pipeline. He notes the closeness to the 2020 CRISPR prize.
responses.response: I agree the Liu-lab trio is the most coherent attribution on the list and that base editing is a chemically elegant concept. My reservation is the one Linke raises himself. Base editing builds on a tool class recognised in 2020, and it is still being assessed for bystander edits and clinical durability. The concept is an engineering advance on a recognised platform, whereas condensation changes how we think about cellular organisation. I would not call B060 a bad choice. I would put it in a different category from a new principle, and I would want the committee to say openly which kind of discovery it wants to reward this year.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing first and PROTACs second, and values converting biological enzyme chemistry into defined, programmable chemical reactions with genome-maintenance relevance. He also stresses that the Target-AID work (Kondo, Nishida) was parallel and independent.
responses.response: I share the view that a prize should honour chemistry with a defined mechanism, and I accept that point for B060. But the Target-AID question shows how fragile the three-name attribution is. If a real parallel contribution cannot be accommodated, the configuration is weaker than it looks. I would also ask Chabes whether the mechanism-level clarity of base editing is really greater than that of phase separation, given the off-target deamination and bystander-edit issues he lists himself. My own uncertainty on B061 is the physiological-relevance debate, and I do not claim it is smaller than his.

responses.point: Aili ranks PROTACs/molecular glues first as induced proximity, a general chemical design principle that opens undruggable targets, and ranks lipid nanoparticles (B019) second as molecular design that reached billions of people.
responses.response: I agree with Aili on B019 and have it second myself. Ionizable lipid self-assembly is molecular design with clear clinical reach. Our shared difficulty is the one he names, the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside modification, plus a credit spread across Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer. On B012 I think his own point about the glue/PROTAC split matters. Handa's cereblon result and Crews and Deshaies's concept are distinct lineages. I would want to know whether Aili thinks a fair three-person split exists without cutting Ciulli, because I do not see one.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first, as a new bond-forming capability with decades of consequences, and ranks PROTACs second. He regards recognition as overdue and the work as distinct from the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
responses.response: I find the maturity and attribution case for Buchwald and Hartwig persuasive, and I do not think the 2010 overlap is disqualifying, since C-N coupling is a distinct, ligand-enabled advance. Where I differ is on how to weigh it against the other candidates. Overdue is an argument about timing and not about conceptual novelty, and the committee has recognised cross-coupling chemistry before. As a physical chemist I want that field fairly represented relative to synthesis. I would not block B055 but I do not rank it above B061.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the physiological relevance of condensates well enough to treat the principle as established rather than a hypothesis still under test.
Whether Rosen or the Pappu and Mittag pair is the better third name, and whether any three-name split is defensible.
Whether a Chemistry framing is robust against a Physiology or Medicine framing for work that began in cell biology.
Whether B060 and B012, the opening leaders, will hold up once the attribution problems (Target-AID; PROTAC versus glue lineages) are examined.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional connection to the credited candidates is apparent from my profile, so I see no recusal issue. I note only scientific proximity: condensates touch the soft-matter and lipid-protein assembly field I work in, and B019 overlaps directly with my own area of lipid self-assembly. I flag that for the committee to judge.
